definition: The layered arrangement of storage in a computer: small, fast, expensive memories (registers, L1, L2, L3 caches) close to the processor, backed by larger, slower, cheaper ones (DRAM, then SSD or disk). Locality lets most accesses be served by the fast upper levels.
example: A load first checks L1, then L2, then L3, and only goes to DRAM if all three miss.

definition: A small, fast memory built into the processor that keeps copies of recently used parts of main memory, so most loads and stores avoid the much slower trip to DRAM. It is managed automatically by hardware, in fixed-size blocks called cache lines. More generally, any small fast store that keeps copies of data to avoid a slower fetch is called a cache, such as a branch-target or decoded-instruction cache.
example: A typical core has its own L1 and L2 caches and shares an L3 with other cores.

definition: The tendency of programs to reuse the same data soon (temporal locality) and to use data near what they used recently (spatial locality). It is the reason a small cache can serve most accesses.
example: A loop summing an array has spatial locality; its running total has temporal locality.

definition: Locality in time: data used recently is likely to be used again soon. Caches exploit it by keeping recently used data and evicting data that has not been used for a while.
example: A loop counter is read and written on every iteration, so it stays in a register or L1.

definition: Locality in space: after using one address, a program is likely to use nearby addresses soon. Caches exploit it by fetching a whole cache line (often 64 bytes) rather than single bytes.
example: Reading element 0 of an array of doubles also brings elements 1 to 7 into the cache in the same 64-byte line.

definition: Solid-state drive: persistent storage built from flash memory. It keeps data without power and is far faster than a spinning hard disk, but much slower than DRAM, and is reached through the I/O system rather than by ordinary loads.
An access whose data is already present in the cache level being checked, so it is served there without going further down the hierarchy.
The fraction of accesses to a cache level that hit: hits divided by accesses. It is often written as a percentage, and it is always one minus the miss rate.
example: 950 hits out of 1,000 accesses is a hit rate of 95 %.

definition: The fraction of accesses to a cache level that miss: misses divided by accesses, equal to one minus the hit rate. A level's local miss rate counts only the accesses that reached that level; its global miss rate counts them against every access the processor made.
example: A streaming scan of 4-byte ints with 64-byte lines has a miss rate of 1/16 = 6.25 %.

definition: The extra time a cache miss costs compared with a hit: the time to get the line from the next level down. It is measured in clock cycles or nanoseconds.
example: If L1 hits take 4 cycles and fetching from L2 adds 10 more, the L1 miss penalty is 10 cycles.

definition: The data (and code) a program actually touches over a short window of time. If the working set fits in a cache level, repeated accesses can hit there; once it grows past that level's capacity, misses rise sharply.
example: A loop that repeatedly scans a 16 KiB table has a 16 KiB working set, which fits in a 32 KiB L1.

definition: A sudden jump in time per operation when some limit is crossed, such as a working set outgrowing a cache level. Graphs of access time against data size show a step at each cache capacity.
The standard, reference implementation of the Python language, written in C. Its lists store references (pointers) to separately allocated objects rather than the values themselves.
A compiler optimisation that replaces a function call with a copy of the function's body. It removes call overhead but enlarges code, which can hurt instruction-cache hit rates.
An electronic component that stores electric charge. In DRAM each bit is a tiny capacitor whose charged or discharged state represents 1 or 0.

The distance in bytes (or elements) between consecutive accesses. Stride 1 (consecutive elements) uses every byte of each cache line; a large stride, such as a whole row, touches a new line on every access.
example: Walking down a column of a 1024 × 1024 array of doubles has a stride of 8,192 bytes.

definition: A loop transformation that splits a large computation, such as a matrix multiply, into small square tiles that fit in the cache together, and finishes all the work on those tiles before moving on. This turns repeated trips to memory into cache hits.
example: Choosing 32 × 32 tiles of doubles keeps three tiles (24 KiB) within a 32 KiB L1.

definition: Swapping the nesting order of loops, for example so the inner loop walks along a row instead of down a column. It does the same work with a different memory access pattern.
example: Changing ijk to ikj cuts model misses in matrix multiply from 1.125 to 0.25 per iteration.

definition: Combining two loops that walk the same data into one loop, so each element is used for both jobs while it is still in the cache instead of being streamed from memory twice.

Array of structures: a data layout where each record's fields are stored together, one record after another. Good when code uses most fields of a record at once; wasteful when a pass touches only one or two fields.
example: A 32-byte Particle struct in an array: a pass that reads only x and vx uses 8 of every 32 bytes fetched.

definition: Structure of arrays: a data layout where each field has its own dense array. A pass over one field touches only that field's bytes and suits SIMD vectorisation.
example: Separate x[] and vx[] arrays mean a pass doing x += vx × dt uses every byte it fetches.

definition: Reorganising a data structure so the frequently used (hot) fields sit together in a compact struct and the rarely used (cold) fields are moved elsewhere, such as behind a pointer. More useful records then fit in each cache line.
The 64-bit (8-byte) IEEE 754 floating-point format, called double in C and float64 in NumPy, with about 15 to 17 significant decimal digits.
example: A 64-byte cache line holds 8 doubles.

definition: The 32-bit (4-byte) IEEE 754 floating-point format, called float in C, with about 7 significant decimal digits. Using it instead of double halves a field's size where the precision is enough.
A long-established programming language for numerical and scientific computing. Its arrays are column-major, and its indices start at 1 by default.
A commercial numerical computing environment and language. Like Fortran, it stores matrices in column-major order.
A high-performance programming language for numerical computing. Its arrays are column-major, like Fortran's.

Fast Fourier transform: an efficient algorithm for converting a signal into its frequency components. Its classic forms work on power-of-two sizes, whose power-of-two strides can cause cache set conflicts, so implementations sometimes pad arrays.
An open-source columnar file format for analytics data, storing values grouped by column so a query reading a few columns reads only those bytes.
Storing a table column by column rather than row by row, the database counterpart of SoA. Scans that touch a few columns read far fewer bytes.

Combining two matrices so each result element is the sum of products of a row of the first and a column of the second. For n × n matrices it takes n³ multiply-adds, and its loop order strongly affects cache behaviour.
Bringing one whole cache line into a cache from the level below, usually because of a miss. Counting fills is a simple way to model memory traffic.
example: Reading 4,000,000 bytes sequentially with 64-byte lines takes 62,500 line fills.

definition: A cache that does not yet hold the data a program needs, for example at start-up, so the first access to each line misses. After warm-up, the useful lines are resident.

Wrapping a primitive value such as an int in a separate heap object (for example Java's Integer). A collection of boxed values holds pointers to scattered objects, adding indirection and object headers.
Java's resizable list class. It stores references to objects, so an ArrayList of Integer holds pointers to boxed Integer objects rather than raw ints.

C++ standard library containers: std::vector keeps its elements contiguously in one buffer, while std::list is a doubly linked list with separately allocated nodes. Scanning a vector has far better spatial locality.
A cache coherence protocol giving each cache line one of four states: Modified, Exclusive, Shared or Invalid. Its Exclusive state lets a core write data nobody else holds without sending a request.
example: A line read by one core alone arrives in E; a later write changes it silently to M.

definition: The simplest common coherence protocol, with three states: Modified, Shared and Invalid. Without an Exclusive state, reading then writing private data costs two requests.

An extension of MESI with a fifth state, Owned: dirty data that other caches may also share. The owner supplies the data to readers and remains responsible for writing it back, deferring a write to memory.
An extension of MESI with a fifth state, Forward: among several caches holding a Shared copy, the one in F answers requests, so a read gets one reply instead of many.
The MESI state meaning this cache holds the only copy of the line and has written it, so the copy below is stale. It must be written back or handed over before another cache can use the line.
The MESI state meaning this cache holds the only copy of the line and it is clean (matches memory). The core can write it without telling anyone, moving it to Modified.
The MESI state meaning the line is clean and other caches may also hold copies. Reads hit locally, but a write must first invalidate the other copies.
The MESI state meaning the cache entry holds no usable data for that line, so any access to it misses.
The extra MOESI state: the line is dirty but other caches may hold Shared copies. The owner supplies data to readers and is responsible for the eventual write-back.
The extra MESIF state: one of several clean Shared copies, designated to answer requests for the line so that only one cache replies.
Bus read: the textbook coherence request a cache broadcasts when it wants to read a line it does not hold. A cache holding the line in Modified supplies the data and moves to Shared.

Bus read exclusive: the textbook coherence request a cache sends when it wants to write a line it does not hold. It fetches the line and makes every other cache invalidate its copy (a read for ownership).
Bus upgrade: the textbook coherence request a cache sends when it already holds a line in Shared and wants to write it. Other caches invalidate their copies; no data needs transferring.
A coherence approach in which a core must invalidate all other copies of a line before writing it, so it becomes the only holder. MESI and its variants are write-invalidate protocols.
A coherence approach in which a write sends the new data to every cache holding a copy, instead of invalidating them. It can cost more traffic when one core writes repeatedly.

The rules for the order in which writes to different memory locations become visible to other cores. Coherence covers one location; the consistency model (such as x86-TSO or Arm's weaker model) covers ordering across locations.

The memory consistency model of x86 processors: stores become visible in program order, but a later load may be satisfied before an earlier store to a different address becomes visible to other cores.
A coherence method in which every request is broadcast and every cache checks its own tags to see whether it holds the line. Simple for a few cores, but broadcast traffic grows with core count.
A coherence method in which a directory records which caches hold, or might hold, each line, so invalidations go only to those caches instead of being broadcast. It scales to many cores and sockets.
A hardware structure that tracks which cores might hold a line, so most coherence requests are sent only where needed rather than broadcast to every cache.
A cache miss caused because another core's write invalidated a line this cache previously held. It is a fourth kind of miss, beyond compulsory, capacity and conflict misses.
Several threads genuinely reading and writing the same variable, such as one shared counter. Unlike false sharing, padding cannot fix it; the program must reduce how often it writes the shared data.
A cache line repeatedly bouncing between cores' caches because they take turns writing it, each write invalidating the other copy. It is the cost behind both true and false sharing.

Arm's Advanced Microcontroller Bus Architecture (AMBA) Coherent Hub Interface: an on-chip interconnect protocol for coherent multicore systems. It uses its own state names (such as Unique/Shared and Clean/Dirty) for the same ideas as MESI.
The wiring and protocol that connects cores, caches and memory controllers on a chip (and between chips), carrying coherence requests and data.
An atomic read with no ordering guarantee beyond the atomicity of the value itself (memory_order_relaxed in C and C++). It is safe against data races yet cheap, so it suits polling a lock.

Memory-ordering rules for synchronisation: an acquire operation (such as taking a lock) stops later accesses moving before it, and a release operation (such as unlocking) stops earlier accesses moving after it.
A lock that waiting threads acquire by looping (spinning) until it becomes free, rather than sleeping. Under contention a naive one generates heavy coherence traffic.

A spinlock technique: waiters spin on an ordinary atomic read of the lock, which hits in their own Shared copy, and only attempt the expensive atomic exchange when the lock looks free. This cuts coherence traffic compared with spinning on the exchange.
A queue-based spinlock (named after Mellor-Crummey and Scott) in which each waiter spins on its own node, so a release disturbs only the next waiter instead of every contender.
A part of a program that accesses shared data and must be run by only one thread at a time, usually protected by a lock.
A variable each thread updates on its own (for example a local count), combined with the others only at the end. It removes shared writes, and so the cache-line ping-pong they cause.

A counter split into several cells that different threads update, with the total found by adding the cells. It spreads writes over several cache lines to reduce contention; Java's LongAdder works this way.
A Java class that keeps a running sum in several striped cells to reduce contention among updating threads. Its sum() adds the cells and is not an atomic snapshot while updates continue.
A Java class holding a 64-bit integer that can be updated atomically. Many threads incrementing one AtomicLong all contend for one cache line.
A Rust type from the crossbeam-utils library that pads and aligns a value to a cache-line-sized boundary to prevent false sharing; on x86-64 it uses 128 bytes.

A C++17 constant giving an implementation-chosen minimum distance to keep independently written objects apart to avoid false sharing. It is a compile-time hint, not a measurement of the machine running the program.

A Java annotation (sun.misc.Contended in Java 8, jdk.internal.vm.annotation.Contended from Java 9) that asks the HotSpot JVM to pad a field or class onto its own cache line(s) to avoid false sharing. By default the JVM honours it only inside the JDK; application classes need the JVM flag -XX:-RestrictContended (and, from Java 9, access to the internal package).
Hit Modified: an Intel performance event for a load that finds its line Modified in another core's cache. Many HITM events on one line are a sign of false or true sharing; perf c2c reports them.

A hardware prefetch behaviour on some processors that, on fetching one 64-byte line, also fetches its neighbour so the pair forms an aligned 128-byte block. It can make two adjacent lines behave like one for false sharing.
The physical mount for a processor chip on a motherboard. A multi-socket server has several processor chips, each with its own memory, joined by an interconnect.
POSIX threads: the standard C threading API on Unix-like systems, providing thread creation, joining and locks.
The circuit, now usually on the CPU chip, that turns cache misses into DRAM commands and schedules them on the memory channels.
A group of cache slots (ways) that a given memory line is allowed to occupy. The index bits of an address choose the set; the line can then sit in any way of that set.
example: A 32 KiB, 8-way cache with 64-byte lines has 64 cache sets of 8 ways each.

definition: One slot within a cache set that can hold a single line. The number of ways per set is the cache's associativity.
example: In an 8-way cache each set has 8 ways, so 8 lines that map to the same set can be cached at once.

definition: The number of places (ways) in a cache where a given memory line may be stored. Higher associativity reduces conflict misses but needs more tag comparators and power.
example: A direct-mapped cache has associativity 1; a 12-way cache lets each line choose among 12 slots.

definition: A cache in which every memory line has exactly one possible slot, chosen by its index bits. It is simple and fast but two busy lines with the same index keep evicting each other.
example: In a 1 KiB direct-mapped cache with 16-byte lines, addresses 1 KiB apart always fight over the same slot.

definition: A cache divided into sets, where a memory line maps to one set but may occupy any of that set's several ways. It is the usual compromise between direct-mapped and fully associative designs.
example: A 2-way set-associative cache lets two lines with the same index coexist instead of evicting each other.

definition: A cache with a single set, so any memory line can be placed in any slot. It has no conflict misses but must compare a tag against every entry, so it is usually only practical for small structures such as TLBs.
example: A fully associative LRU cache of the same capacity is the reference used to separate capacity misses from conflict misses.

definition: The high-order address bits stored alongside each cached line. Because many memory lines share one set, the cache compares the requested address's tag with the stored tags to tell which line is actually present.
example: For a 48-bit address with 6 offset and 6 index bits, each line stores a 36-bit tag.

definition: The address bits just above the offset that select which cache set to look in. With S sets it is log base 2 of S bits wide, for example 6 bits for 64 sets.
example: With 64-byte lines and 64 sets, address bits 6 to 11 form the set index.

definition: The lowest address bits, which select a byte within a cache line. A line of L bytes needs log base 2 of L offset bits, for example 6 bits for a 64-byte line.
example: In address 0x678 with 64-byte lines, the low 6 bits 111000 give offset 56.

definition: A status bit stored with each cache line saying whether the slot holds real data. A tag match only counts as a hit if the valid bit is set, so an empty cache never returns garbage.
example: At power-on every valid bit is 0, so the first access to each line misses.

definition: A status bit in a write-back cache marking a line that has been modified since it was fetched. A dirty line must be written back to the next level before its slot can be reused.
example: Evicting a clean line just discards it; evicting a dirty line costs a write-back of 64 bytes.

definition: A cache miss on the very first access to an item (in a CPU cache, a line), which no cache size or associativity can avoid. Prefetching can hide it by fetching the line before it is demanded.
example: Reading a fresh 64 KiB array of 64-byte lines causes at least 1,024 compulsory misses.

definition: A miss on a previously used line that would also miss in a fully associative cache of the same size, because the program's working set is bigger than the cache. Bigger caches or better locality (such as blocking) reduce them.
example: Repeatedly scanning a 64 KiB array through a 32 KiB cache causes capacity misses on every pass.

definition: A miss on a previously used line that a fully associative cache of the same size would have hit, caused by too many busy lines mapping to the same set. More associativity or padding addresses can reduce them.
example: Two arrays exactly 32 KiB apart in a 32 KiB direct-mapped cache evict each other on every access: conflict misses.

definition: Mark Hill's classification of cache misses into compulsory, capacity and conflict misses. Knowing which kind dominates tells you whether a bigger cache, more associativity or better access patterns would help.
example: If a miss disappears in a same-size fully associative cache, it was a conflict miss.

definition: The rule a cache uses to pick which line in a full set to evict (the victim) when a new line must be brought in. Common choices are LRU, pseudo-LRU, RRIP-style and random.
example: With 8 ways and LRU, the line untouched for longest in that set is evicted.

definition: The line a cache chooses to evict to make room for a newly fetched line. Which line becomes the victim is decided by the replacement policy.
example: In a direct-mapped cache there is no choice: the single occupant of the slot is the victim.

definition: A cheap approximation of least-recently-used replacement. Tree-PLRU keeps a binary tree of bits per set (ways minus one bits, so 7 for 8 ways) that point away from recently used ways; it can pick a different victim from true LRU.
example: An 8-way set with tree-PLRU needs 7 bits, whereas recording the exact LRU order of 8 ways needs at least 16 bits (there are 40,320 possible orders).

definition: Re-reference interval prediction: a family of replacement policies that give each line a small counter predicting how soon it will be reused. New lines start with a 'distant' prediction, so data touched once by a scan is evicted before data that is reused.
example: Under RRIP, one pass over a huge array does not flush a loop's frequently reused data out of the cache.

definition: A replacement policy that picks the victim way at random (or pseudo-randomly). It needs almost no state and has no pathological pattern, but ignores recency.
example: Random replacement keeps no recency bits at all, so it costs nothing to update on a hit.

definition: A cache that picks its set using bits of the virtual address but compares physical-address tags. If the index and offset fit inside the page offset, the set lookup can start while the TLB translates the address, with no aliasing problems.
example: A 32 KiB, 8-way L1 with 64-byte lines uses 12 index-plus-offset bits, exactly the offset of a 4 KiB page, so it can be VIPT without aliases.

definition: The low address bits that select a byte within a memory page. Address translation never changes them, so they are the same in the virtual and physical address.
example: A 4 KiB page has a 12-bit page offset, because 4,096 is 2 to the power 12.

definition: A circuit that checks whether a stored cache tag equals the tag of the requested address. A set-associative cache needs one per way, all working in parallel.
example: An 8-way cache compares 8 tags at once on every lookup.

definition: The power you must raise 2 to in order to get a given number, written log_2: how many 2s multiplied together make it. It tells you how many bits are needed to number a power-of-two count of things.
example: log_2(64) = 6, so 6 bits number 64 bytes in a line.

definition: The remainder after whole-number division, written mod. Simple caches choose a set as the line number mod the number of sets, which for a power-of-two set count is just the low bits of the line number.

A cache that updates only its own copy on a store, marks the line dirty, and writes it to the next level later, for example when it is evicted or another core requests it. This saves traffic when a line is written many times.
example: A loop incrementing a counter 1,000 times writes it back to L2 once, at eviction.

definition: Adding unused space to rows or arrays so their addresses spread across different cache sets instead of colliding. It trades a little memory for fewer conflict misses.
example: Padding each 8,192-byte row by 64 bytes spreads a column walk over all 64 sets.

definition: Average memory access time: the expected time one memory access takes, counting fast cache hits and slower misses together. In the simple blocking model it is the hit time plus the miss rate times the miss penalty.
example: A 4-cycle L1 that misses 5% of the time with a 100-cycle miss penalty has an AMAT of 4 + 0.05 × 100 = 9 cycles.

definition: The time a cache takes to look up an address and return the data when it is present. In the AMAT model it is paid on every access to that level, hit or miss, because the cache is always checked first.
example: An L1 data cache typically has a hit time of about 4 to 5 clock cycles.

definition: A cache level's misses divided by the accesses that actually reach that level. For L2 these are only the L1 misses, so the number can look high even when few accesses go to main memory.
example: If 50,000 accesses reach L2 and 10,000 miss, L2's local miss rate is 20%.

definition: A cache level's misses divided by all memory accesses the processor made. It equals the product of the local miss rates from L1 down to that level, and tells you how often an access goes beyond that level.
example: With L1 missing 5% and L2 missing 20% locally, L2's global miss rate is 0.05 × 0.20 = 1%.

definition: A cache write policy in which every store updates the cached copy and is also sent on to the next level, possibly via a write buffer. Lines never hold data that the next level lacks once pending writes drain, so no dirty bit is needed.
example: Three stores to x in a row send three writes to L2 under write-through, but only one eventual write under write-back.

definition: A cache write policy in which a write updates only the cache's copy and marks it dirty; the new data is passed down to the next level later, for example when the line is evicted or another core requests it. It saves traffic when the same data is written repeatedly.
example: A million stores to one resident 64-byte line cause a single 64-byte write-back under write-back, versus 8 MB of forwarded 8-byte stores under write-through without merging.

definition: A small queue that holds stores on their way to the next memory level, so the processor does not have to wait for each one to complete. It can merge several stores to the same line, and a full buffer stalls further stores.
A buffer that holds a dirty line being evicted, so the cache can fetch the missing line first and write the old one back afterwards. This takes the write-back off the critical path of the miss.
example: If 40% of victims are dirty and each write-back costs 100 cycles, a write-back buffer that hides them all cuts the average miss penalty from 140 to 100 cycles.

definition: A write-miss policy in which a store to a line not in the cache first allocates (and usually fetches) that line, then updates it in the cache. It suits data that will be read or written again soon and is the usual partner of write-back.

A write-miss policy in which a store that misses is sent straight to the next level without bringing the line into the cache. It suits data that will not be touched again and is the usual partner of write-through.

A coherence request that fetches a cache line and at the same time gains exclusive permission to write it, invalidating copies in other caches. A store that misses in a write-allocate cache usually issues one.

A lower cache level that is guaranteed to hold a copy of every line held in the upper levels it covers. Evicting a line from it forces those upper copies to be invalidated; in return it can filter coherence snoops, at the cost of duplicated capacity.
A cache arrangement in which a line lives in only one of the specified levels at a time, so their capacities add up without duplication. Lines typically move between levels on misses and evictions.
Non-inclusive, non-exclusive: a cache hierarchy that guarantees neither inclusion nor exclusion, so a line being present or absent in one level says nothing certain about another.

Cycles in which the processor cannot make progress because it is waiting for data from the memory hierarchy. In a blocking model they are the references per instruction times the miss rate times the miss penalty.

A cache (or performance model) in which the processor waits for a miss to be served before doing anything else, so misses are handled one at a time and their full latency is exposed. Modern out-of-order cores use non-blocking caches instead.
Logic in the processor that spots access patterns, such as walking through an array, and fetches lines into the cache before the program asks for them, turning some misses into hits.

A store instruction that writes data towards memory without allocating it in the cache or reading the old line first, typically gathering full lines in write-combining buffers. It suits large buffers that will not be read again soon.
example: Overwriting a 64 MiB buffer with ordinary write-allocate stores moves about 128 MiB of DRAM data; ideal full-line streaming stores move about 64 MiB.

definition: A small buffer that gathers several stores to the same line so they can be sent to memory as one full-line write. Streaming stores use it to avoid reading the old line.
Combining several pending stores to the same cache line in a write buffer into a single transfer to the next level, reducing write-through traffic.
Removing a line from a cache to make room for a new one; the line chosen is called the victim. In a write-back cache a dirty victim must be written back first.
The latency of the slowest small fraction of operations, such as the worst 1%. An average such as AMAT can look good while a few very slow accesses dominate the run time.

The storage element for one bit in DRAM: one transistor acting as a switch and one capacitor holding a small charge. Reading it disturbs the charge, and the charge leaks away, which is why DRAM needs sense amplifiers and refresh.
A DDR5 refresh mode that refreshes one chosen bank in each bank group at a time, so the other banks can keep serving requests, subject to timing rules.
A line of cells in a DRAM bank that is opened (activated) all at once into the row buffer; typically thousands of bits wide. Not the same thing as an operating-system page.
A DRAM access to the row already open in the bank's row buffer. It needs only a READ command, so its cost is the CAS latency.
A DRAM access to a bank with no row open. The controller must activate the row and then read it, costing tRCD plus CL.
A DRAM access to a bank whose row buffer holds a different row. The controller must precharge (close) it, activate the wanted row and then read, costing tRP plus tRCD plus CL: the slowest case.

A set of DRAM chips on a module that are operated together to fill the full width of the channel, for example eight 8-bit-wide chips for a 64-bit channel. Ranks on one channel take turns using the bus.

An independent array inside a DRAM chip with its own row buffer, so different banks can have different rows open and work in parallel. DDR4 and DDR5 also gather banks into bank groups with their own timing rules.
example: A DDR4 x8 chip has 16 banks in 4 bank groups.

definition: Dual in-line memory module: the small circuit board of DRAM chips that plugs into a motherboard slot. A DIMM carries one or more ranks.
In DDR5, one of the two independent 32-bit halves of a DIMM's 64-bit data interface. Each has its own commands, so the controller can run two accesses at once on one module.

Transferring data on both the rising and the falling edge of a clock, so two transfers happen per clock cycle; it is what DDR stands for. The number in a name like DDR4-3200 is the transfer rate in MT/s, twice the clock frequency in MHz.
example: DDR4-3200 makes 3,200 million transfers per second on a 1,600 MHz clock.

definition: Mega-transfers per second: millions of data transfers on a bus each second. For DDR memory it is twice the clock frequency in MHz, because data moves twice per clock.
example: DDR5-4800 runs at 4,800 MT/s on a 2,400 MHz clock.

definition: Column address strobe latency: the number of memory clock cycles between a READ command to an open row and the first data appearing. It is quoted in cycles, so its time in nanoseconds depends on the clock speed.
example: DDR4-3200 CL22 means 22 cycles of 0.625 ns, which is 13.75 ns.

aliases: row address to column address delay
definition: Row-to-column delay: the minimum number of clock cycles between activating a DRAM row and reading a column from it.
Row precharge time: the minimum number of clock cycles needed to close the open row in a bank (precharge) before another row can be activated.
The DRAM activate command: it opens a row, copying it from the cells into the bank's row buffer so its columns can be read.
The DRAM precharge command: it closes the open row in a bank and resets the bit lines so another row can be activated.
The DRAM read command: it reads a burst of data from columns of the row currently open in a bank.
The number of consecutive data transfers one DRAM read or write produces. DDR4 uses 8 (BL8) on a 64-bit bus and DDR5 uses 16 (BL16) on a 32-bit sub-channel; both deliver 64 bytes, one cache line.
First-ready, first-come first-served: a memory-controller scheduling policy that serves requests hitting an already open row first, then the oldest request. It raises row-hit rates and bandwidth.
The maximum rate a memory channel can move data, equal to its data-transfer rate times its bus width. Real programs reach less because of refresh, row-buffer conflicts and too few requests in flight.
example: DDR4-3200 on a 64-bit channel: 3,200 million × 8 bytes = 25.6 GB/s.

definition: A queueing result: in a steady state, the average number of items in a system equals their arrival rate times the average time each spends inside. For memory, bandwidth equals bytes in flight divided by latency.
example: 64 lines of 64 bytes in flight with 80 ns latency sustain 51.2 GB/s.

definition: Memory requests that have been issued but whose data has not yet returned. The more that can be outstanding at once, the more of the memory latency is overlapped and the higher the achievable bandwidth.
Following a chain of pointers, as in a linked list, where each address is only known after the previous load returns. Misses cannot overlap, so it runs at memory latency rather than bandwidth.
Non-uniform memory access: a design where each processor socket (or node) has its own local memory and reaching another node's memory takes longer. Where data is placed therefore affects performance.

On a NUMA machine, local memory is attached to the same socket or node as the core using it; remote memory belongs to another node and is reached over the inter-socket link, usually with higher latency.
Ultra Path Interconnect: Intel's point-to-point link between processor sockets, carrying remote memory accesses and coherence traffic.
AMD's interconnect between the dies and sockets of its processors, carrying memory and coherence traffic.

Linux's default NUMA placement: a page gets physical memory on the node of the CPU that first writes it (faults it in), not the one that called malloc. Initialising data with the threads that will use it places it locally.
Linux command-line tools for NUMA: numactl runs a program with a chosen CPU and memory placement policy and shows the node layout; numastat reports per-node memory allocation statistics.
A NUMA policy that spreads a program's pages round-robin across nodes, balancing placement for large shared data at the cost of some remote accesses.
A Linux kernel feature that samples which nodes access each page and migrates pages towards the threads using them, at the cost of extra page faults.

An Intel hardware prefetcher that can use values loaded from memory to predict the addresses of later loads in some indirect-access patterns, unlike stream or stride prefetchers that only see addresses.
How many loop iterations ahead a software prefetch asks for data. It should be roughly the memory latency divided by the time per iteration, so the data arrives just before it is needed.
example: With 100 ns latency and 5 ns per iteration, a distance of about 20 iterations is a starting point.

definition: A GCC and Clang built-in function that emits a prefetch hint for a given address. The hint may be ignored, and it does not fault, but computing the address must still be valid C.
Filling a cache with lines that will not be used, such as useless prefetches, which evicts lines that would have been used.
Describes code whose speed is limited by the memory system rather than by computation: bandwidth-limited if it cannot get bytes fast enough, latency-limited if it waits on one miss at a time.
Describes code whose speed is limited by the processor's arithmetic rather than by memory; faster memory or prefetching barely helps it.
High-performance computing: running large scientific or engineering workloads on supercomputers and clusters, where memory bandwidth tuning matters a great deal.
Basic input/output system: the motherboard firmware that starts the computer; its setup screens expose hardware options such as enabling or disabling individual prefetchers.
A page of memory not backed by a file, such as heap or stack memory. On Linux it receives physical memory only when first touched.

In computer architecture, the rate at which data can be moved between parts of the system, such as between DRAM and the caches, usually given in bytes per second (GB/s). It is separate from latency: a memory system can deliver a lot of data per second while each individual access still takes tens of nanoseconds.
example: One DDR4-3200 channel has a peak bandwidth of 25.6 GB/s.

definition: Several cores repeatedly trying to write (or lock) the same cache line at the same time. Each write needs exclusive ownership of the line, so the line keeps moving between caches and the writers slow each other down.
example: Eight threads incrementing one shared atomic counter all contend for the single cache line that holds it.

definition: Reading or writing memory in increasing (or decreasing) address order, one element after the next. It uses every byte of each cache line and is the pattern hardware prefetchers detect most easily.
example: Summing an array from index 0 upwards is a sequential scan.

definition: In computer hardware, one complete request-and-response exchange on a bus or interconnect, such as a cache asking for a line or telling other caches to invalidate theirs. Coherence protocols are described in terms of these transactions.
example: A BusRd is a bus transaction that asks for a copy of a line to read.

definition: In programming, a library type that holds a collection of elements, such as C++ std::vector, Java ArrayList or a Python list. Whether it stores the values themselves or references to them decides its memory layout and cache behaviour.
example: std::vector<double> stores raw doubles contiguously; ArrayList<Integer> stores references to boxed objects.

definition: The rules (line states and messages) by which hardware keeps cache coherence: private caches holding copies of one memory location agree on a single order of writes to it, so a write by one core is eventually seen by the others. In Architecture, 'coherence' on its own means this cache coherence; MESI is the textbook protocol.

The number of bytes in one cache line, the unit a cache stores and moves. It is commonly 64 bytes on current x86 and many Arm processors, with some caches using 128; a 64-byte line is a cache line of that size.
example: A 64-byte line holds 8 doubles or 16 four-byte ints.

definition: A cache miss caused by the program's own load or store, as opposed to a request made by a prefetcher. Prefetching aims to turn demand misses into hits.

Error-correcting code built into each DDR5 DRAM chip, which corrects single-bit errors inside the chip's own storage. It does not protect data on its way to the processor, so it does not replace system-level ECC on the module.

Prefetching requested by explicit hint instructions placed in the program (for example via __builtin_prefetch), rather than detected by hardware. The hint asks for a line early so a later load hits; the processor may ignore it.

A DRAM refresh command that refreshes every bank of a rank at once, so the whole rank is unavailable for the refresh time (tRFC). It contrasts with DDR5 same-bank refresh, which leaves most banks free.
example: With a 350 ns refresh every 7,812.5 ns, an all-bank refresh blocks the rank about 4.5% of the time.

definition: The number of data bits one DRAM chip supplies per transfer, written ×4, ×8 or ×16. Chips are combined to fill a channel: eight ×8 chips make a 64-bit DDR4 rank.
